newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Rexrodt says can live with dlr/mark level.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Rexrodt says can live with dlr/mark level.

text.p: Germany's minister of Economics Gunter Rexrodt said on Friday he could live very well with the current level of the German mark against the U.S. dollar.
He told a news conference in Sydney he still expected German unemployment to average 4.2 million over calendar 1997, despite the rise on Thursday in unemployment to 4.66 million in January.
"I can live very well with the present relationship between the U.S. dollar and the German mark," he said.
The dollar was at 1.6553/63 marks at 0540 GMT on Friday.
Rexrodt would not say if he thought any action should be taken over the dollar's strength at the meeting of G7 ministers in Berlin this weekend.
Rexrodt said his government had forecast in its budget that unemployment would rise until May and then start falling, to create an average of 4.2 million for the full 1997 year.

"We will have a curve that means that we come up to a level we do have now, maybe next month a little bit more, I don't know. But the same dimension, and starting in May it will come down and the average in 1997 will be 4.2 million people," he said.
Asked if he still thought the forecast would be met given the half a million rise for January, he said: "On average, yes."
Rexrodt said the German government had no alternative to continuing its labour reforms, deregulations and privatisations if it wanted to reduce unemployment.
He said the government was committed to meeting its target for deficit reduction necessary to meet its Maastricht treaty obligations to create a European Monetary Union.
Economists have said the much higher than expected unemployment levels and the subsequently higher benefit payouts had increased the risk of not reaching the Maastricht targets.
"We are in a difficult situation without any doubt," Rexrodt said when asked if the higher unemployment endangered the government's plan to cut its deficit to 2.9 percent of GDP.
"We have a trilemma. We have to save money in the budget because we need space for tax reforms," he said.
"We have to fulfill the criterias of Maastricht which means not more than 3.0 percent deficit and we have to fight with the unemployment issue," he said.

"I think we see and approach solutions we need in order to balance this trilemma and I'm sure Germany will fulfill the criterias of Maastricht and thereby deliver the preconditions for European Monetary Union starting January 1st 1999."
Rexrodt said the budget remained on track to meet the deficit target because unemployment would stay within forecasts and therefore there was no need for new budget cuts.
"Now we do have a budget plan that balances the problems in the appropriate way. In our calculation we count the present number of unemployed people."
"This is part of our budget plan and therefore we can base on that in the future as well," he said.
Rexrodt said the unusually cold winter had been a factor in the January rise in unemployment, but the problem was largely a structural one.
"We are in a very strong international competition and the high wage, the welfare countries like Germany have to adapt their structure to this changed world," he said.
"There is only one way we must go and that is continuing our reform policy."
Rexrodt said the government had to continue its reforms of the tax and pension systems and needed more flexibility in the labour market.
He said these reforms were difficult when some opposition groups blocked them in the German parliament.
"There is no alternative. We must go on in this reform policy and I'm sure we will succeed after a particular time."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
